Turn Up
TURN UP
verb / noun (Millennial slang)
From the ordinary phrasal verb turn up (to increase, as the volume), re-coined in late-2000s Southern hip-hop and club culture to mean to party with maximum energy, or to get someone else hyped. As a noun, a turn-up is a wild party or an energetic moment. Lil Jon’s 2000s crunk records set the tone; the 2013 single "Turn Down for What" (DJ Snake and Lil Jon) made the phrase a chant. By the mid-2010s, "turn up" could mean celebration of any kind, including at sports games and graduations.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

To turn up is to raise the energy of a gathering: to party hard, to celebrate loudly, to get everyone hyped. Unlike its cousin turnt, the phrase does not always imply drinking; a team can turn up after a win, and a family can turn up at a wedding. The Christian observation: Scripture is not against turning up. It commands feasting. Israel’s calendar was full of celebrations where God told His people to rejoice before Him with food and music. When the prodigal came home, the father said, "bring hither the fatted calf, and kill it; and let us eat, and be merry" (Luk 15:23). David "danced before the LORD with all his might" (2Sa 6:14). And Nehemiah told a weeping crowd, "Go your way, eat the fat, and drink the sweet … for the joy of the LORD is your strength" (Neh 8:10). The question is not whether to celebrate but before Whom and how. Paul draws the line: "Let us walk honestly, as in the day; not in rioting and drunkenness, not in chambering and wantonness" (Rom 13:13). The Preacher, who tried every kind of party, concluded of mirth, "What doeth it?" (Ecc 2:2) when it is pursued for itself. A father teaches his children to turn up at weddings, birthdays, and Easter, loud and glad, and to avoid the kind of party where the celebration is just the excuse.

Webster 1828 Definition

Millennial hip-hop slang (late 2000s; 2013 "Turn Down for What") for partying or celebrating with maximum energy; Scripture commands joyful feasting before the Lord (Luk 15:23) and forbids rioting and drunkenness (Rom 13:13).

TURN UP, v.i. / n. (Millennial slang, late 2000s–2010s) To party or celebrate with high energy; to hype a crowd. "Time to turn up." A turn-up: a wild party. Related: turnt, "Turn Down for What."

Webster (1828), root turn: TURN, verb transitive [Latin turnus; torniare, to turn; tornare, to return; torneare, tornire, to turn to fence round, to tilt; torniamento, tournament.] 1. To cause to move in a circular course; as, to turn a wheel; to turn a spindle; to turn the body. 2. To change or shift sides; to put the upper side downwards, or one side in the place of the other. It is said a hen turns her eggs often when sitting. 3. To alter, as a position. Expert When to advance, or stand, or turn the sway of battle. 4. To cause to preponderate; […]

Decode for parents: "turning up" can mean innocent celebration or a drinking party; ask where, with whom, and who is in charge.

Key Scripture

Luk 15:23 — "And bring hither the fatted calf, and kill it; and let us eat, and be merry:"

2Sa 6:14 — "And David danced before the LORD with all his might; and David was girded with a linen ephod."

Neh 8:10 — "Then he said unto them, Go your way, eat the fat, and drink the sweet, and send portions unto them for whom nothing is prepared: for this day is holy unto our Lord: neither be ye sorry; for the joy of the LORD is your strength."

Rom 13:13 — "Let us walk honestly, as in the day; not in rioting and drunkenness, not in chambering and wantonness, not in strife and envying."

Ecc 2:2 — "I said of laughter, It is mad: and of mirth, What doeth it?"

Modern Corruption

Turn up can name holy celebration or a riot; Scripture commands feasting before the Lord and forbids the party that is only an excuse for excess.

expand to see more

The corruption is celebration cut loose from anything to celebrate. The Millennial turn-up often has no occasion but the weekend, and its energy has to be supplied chemically or by escalation, because there is no real joy at the centre. Solomon tried that experiment with all his resources and reported the result: "I said of laughter, It is mad: and of mirth, What doeth it?" (Ecc 2:2). Rioting is what celebration becomes when it has nothing to rejoice in.

The recovery is the feast with a reason. The Church’s calendar, its weddings, its baptisms, and its Lord’s Days are occasions for real joy, and Christians should throw the best parties in town: loud singing, long tables, dancing at weddings, children up late. Teach the young that the opposite of a drunken turn-up is not a quiet room but a feast where the Lord is honoured and everyone goes home glad and clear-headed.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Turn + up (increase the volume) → late-2000s crunk and Southern hip-hop turn up → 2013 "Turn Down for What" → general celebration slang.

Late 2000s: crunk and Southern hip-hop turn up — to party hard

2013: DJ Snake and Lil Jon, "Turn Down for What"

Mid-2010s: generalized to any high-energy celebration

Biblical anchor: let us eat, and be merry (Luk 15:23); not in rioting and drunkenness (Rom 13:13)

Usage
